steps.title: Save first, spend the rest
steps.body: Most people save what is left at the end of the month. Often, that is almost nothing. The trick: save first, on payday. Then spend the rest. A small amount moved every day or every month adds up fast: €5 a day becomes €1,825 in one year. The share of your income you keep is your [[savings-rate]].

steps.prompt: Where can a saver find room? Swipe each cost: one you must pay, or one you can change.
steps.explanation: Costs you must pay each month are [[fixed-costs]]. The others are where most people find room to save.

steps.prompt: Two streaming services at €13 each: €26 a month. Cancel them, move the money on payday, and watch what it becomes.

goal.hint: Move the years to 5 or more.

steps.note: €26 a month is €312 a year. Over 5 years it is more than €1,600, without changing anything else.

steps.prompt: It's payday. Which plan makes saving most likely to happen?
options: Move the saving amount on payday, then spend the rest
Spend first, then save what is left
Save only in months when money is left over
steps.explanation: When saving happens first, by a [[standing-order]] on payday, it does not depend on willpower at the end of the month.

steps.prompt: Mia earns €2,000 a month after tax. She saves €300. What is her savings rate?
steps.explanation: €300 of €2,000 is 15%. Your [[savings-rate]] is the share you keep, not the amount. It lets you compare months, even when income changes.

scenes.desc: Saving what is left often means saving nothing. Saving on payday first is the trick. The share you keep is your [[savings-rate]].
